weekLabel: Week 13 · Meeting A · Machine Learning I: Evaluated Prediction (Regression)

slides.title: Real buildings don't hand you a formula. You fit one from what got built.
slides.subtitle: Supervised regression, a naive baseline, and the honest metrics that say how wrong a model still is — scaffolded fast with AI, then audited by hand.
slides.teaching: Open by naming the shift explicitly: Weeks 9 and 11 gave you a clean analytic formula, energy_proxy(wwr, shade_m), that you swept or minimized directly. Radley Hall's 140 explored envelope variants have no such formula — only simulated outcomes. Today you fit a model FROM those outcomes. Preview the leakage bug (est_annual_cost_index) as the core artifact of this whole session, not a bonus.

slides.title: The metric matters more than the fit
slides.statement: Fitting a line through data is the easy part. Knowing — and reporting — exactly how wrong that line still is, is the actual skill.
slides.supporting: An AI assistant will scaffold today's LinearRegression fit/predict pipeline in minutes. The remaining time is about a naive baseline, MAE/RMSE/R², a residual plot, and a real leakage bug hiding in the AI-drafted code — because a fast fit means nothing without an honest evaluation.
slides.teaching: Set the tone for the session: speed of authorship is not the point this week; honesty of evaluation is.

outcomes.head: Distinguish
outcomes.body: Tell a feature apart from a target, and a naive baseline apart from a fitted model.

outcomes.head: Split
outcomes.body: Use train_test_split to hold out data a fitted model never trains on, and explain why that matters.

outcomes.head: Evaluate
outcomes.body: Compute and interpret MAE, RMSE, and R² for a naive baseline and a scikit-learn LinearRegression model, and read a residual plot.

outcomes.head: Audit
outcomes.body: Find and fix a real data-leakage bug in AI-drafted regression code, and explain in words why it was wrong.

slides.teaching: All four map directly onto this week's graded studio assignment (Meeting B) and Project 2 Part IV's required baseline-model checkpoint.

slides.title: From a formula you swept to a model you fit

left.head: Weeks 9 & 11: a clean formula
left.body: energy_proxy(wwr, shade_m) was a formula YOU wrote — swept on a grid (Week 9), then minimized directly (Week 11). Every input produced an exact, known output.

right.head: Week 13: outcomes, no formula
right.body: Radley Hall's design team simulated 140 real envelope variants — nobody wrote down the formula connecting wwr, shade_m, glazing_shgc to energy use. Today you FIT one, from the outcomes alone.

slides.teaching: Point out explicitly: wwr and shade_m are the exact same variables and bounds as Weeks 9/11 — this is deliberate continuity, not a coincidence.

slides.title: radley_portfolio_envelope.csv — 140 explored design variants
rows: V001–V140, one row per explored variant (fictional)
surface-to-volume proxy — added back in Week 14
N/E/S/W facade — diagnosis only, never a feature
reporting-only cost proxy — never a feature
slides.callout: n=140 rows. Today's model uses only 3 columns as FEATURES: wwr, shade_m, glazing_shgc.
slides.teaching: State plainly this dataset is fictional, same convention as Radley Hall in Weeks 4-8 — say so on slide.

slides.title: Feature, defined
slides.definition: An input column a model is allowed to use to make its prediction. Also called a predictor or independent variable.

example.head: wwr, shade_m, glazing_shgc
example.body: Today's three features. The model reads these three columns for every row — nothing else — to produce a predicted eui_kwh_m2yr.

slides.note: compactness and orientation are real columns in this dataset too — but they are NOT features in today's model; only wwr, shade_m, glazing_shgc are. Week 14 adds compactness back in.
slides.teaching: First of a paired pair — target is next slide. Keep this crisp; the pairing is what matters, not the length.

slides.title: Target, defined
slides.definition: The column you are trying to predict. Also called the label or dependent variable.

example.head: eui_kwh_m2yr
example.body: Today's target — the simulated annual energy-use-intensity proxy every one of the 140 design variants actually achieved.

slides.note: est_annual_cost_index is neither a feature nor the target today — it LOOKS like it could be a feature. That is exactly the trap this deck ends on.
slides.teaching: Foreshadow the leakage bug explicitly here — est_annual_cost_index resembles a legitimate feature but is actually derived from the target itself.

slides.title: Supervised, defined
slides.definition: The training data already includes the correct target value for every row. The model learns from known answers, not from trial and error.

example.head: All 140 variants have a real eui_kwh_m2yr
example.body: Every row in radley_portfolio_envelope.csv already carries its simulated energy result — that known answer is what makes this supervised learning.

slides.teaching: Pair with regression next — supervised describes the DATA, regression describes the TARGET's type.

slides.title: Regression, defined
slides.definition: Predicting a CONTINUOUS numeric target — the value can be 22.4, 31.8, or anything in between, not just one of a fixed set of categories.

example.head: eui_kwh_m2yr is continuous
example.body: kWh/m2/yr can land anywhere on a number line — as opposed to classification, which predicts a category (meets_code: yes/no, Week 14).

slides.teaching: Keep this distinction crisp; Week 14 will contrast it directly against classification on the exact same underlying physical process.

slides.title: train_test_split, defined
slides.definition: Randomly holds out a fraction of rows (test_size=0.25 → 25%) as a TEST set the model never trains on; the rest becomes the TRAINING set used to fit it. random_state=42 fixes exactly which rows land in each set, so the split is reproducible.

example.head: Why hold out data at all
example.body: A model evaluated on the SAME rows it was fit on can look better than it really is — it may have partly memorized those rows instead of learning the pattern. You need rows it has never seen to get an honest score.

slides.note: random_state=42 is the fixed seed used for EVERY split in this three-week block — same convention as fixed seeds in Weeks 9-12.
slides.teaching: Name random_state=42 explicitly as the reproducibility convention for this whole block before moving to the anatomy slide.

slides.title: train_test_split, one call at a time

parts.label: The function
parts.body: Splits X and y together, row-aligned, into train/test pairs.

parts.label: Features + target
parts.body: wwr, shade_m, glazing_shgc (features, X) and eui_kwh_m2yr (target, y).

parts.label: Held-out fraction
parts.body: 25% of rows — 35 of 140 — become the test set.

parts.label: Reproducibility seed
parts.body: Same 105/35 split every time this line runs.

slides.teaching: Walk the parts in call order: the function, then X and y (what goes in), then the two keyword arguments (how it splits). This is the exact call the next slide runs.

slides.title: Splitting Radley Hall's 140 variants, 105/35
slides.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

FEATURES3 = ["wwr", "shade_m", "glazing_shgc"]
X = df[FEATURES3]
y = df["eui_kwh_m2yr"]

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)

print(X_train.shape, X_test.shape)
slides.explainHead: 105 rows to learn from, 35 to judge with
slides.explainBody: test_size=0.25 reserves 35 of 140 rows purely for evaluation. Every metric for the rest of today's lecture is computed on THESE 35 rows only — rows the model never touched while fitting. Naming the list FEATURES3 once, instead of retyping three column names, is what lets every later slide refit the SAME three features without a copy-paste error.
slides.teaching: Verified by running against the pinned course environment: shapes print exactly (105, 3) (35, 3).

slides.title: Naive baseline, defined
slides.definition: The simplest possible prediction rule that still uses the target — here, DummyRegressor(strategy="mean"): predict the SAME training-set mean EUI for every test row, ignoring wwr/shade_m/shgc entirely.

example.head: Why it comes first
example.body: If a real model cannot beat "just guess the average," it has told you something real — either it is not learning the pattern, or the pattern is not learnable from these features. Build the baseline BEFORE the real model, every time.

slides.teaching: This ordering — baseline before model — is the plan's explicit opening move for Week 13; do not skip it to get to LinearRegression faster.

slides.title: One helper function, reused for every model today
slides.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score

def report_metrics(y_true, y_pred, label: str) -> dict:
    """Print and return MAE, RMSE and R2."""
    mae = mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred)
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred))
    r2 = r2_score(y_true, y_pred)
    line = f"MAE={mae:.4f} RMSE={rmse:.4f} R2={r2:.5f}"
    print(label + ":", line)
    return {"MAE": mae, "RMSE": rmse, "R2": r2}
slides.explainHead: Write the scoring once, reuse it four times
slides.explainBody: Defining a function prints nothing — this cell just stores it. Four models today (baseline, 3-feature, AI-drafted, fixed) get scored by this one function, so none can be quietly scored a different way. Note the convention required on every function since Week 4: a one-line docstring in triple quotes, plus type hints — label: str means label must be text, -> dict means a dictionary comes back.
slides.teaching: Verified against the pinned course environment. Point at each of the three convention pieces by name (docstring, parameter type hint, return type hint) before running anything — this is the first function students write in the machine-learning block and it sets the pattern for Project 2.

slides.title: The naive baseline: predict the mean, every time
slides.code:
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor

baseline = DummyRegressor(strategy="mean")
baseline.fit(X_train, y_train)
pred_base = baseline.predict(X_test)

print("predicts:", round(pred_base[0], 4))
base = report_metrics(y_test, pred_base, "baseline")
slides.explainHead: R²≈0 is not "bad" — it's the definition
slides.explainBody: R²=-0.00003 for a mean-only predictor is R² essentially exactly 0 by construction — this IS what "no better than guessing the average" looks like, numerically. Every model from here on is judged against this exact number. The helper also hands the three values back as a dictionary, so base["MAE"] is available later without retyping 2.8906.
slides.teaching: Verified against the pinned course environment: predicts 28.0836, MAE 2.8906, RMSE 3.8154, R2 -0.00003 — matches data/README.md exactly.

slides.title: Scaffold with AI, then audit

left.head: Why use AI here
left.body: The plan's own instruction: use an AI coding assistant to scaffold the LinearRegression fit/predict pipeline QUICKLY — this course is not testing whether you can hand-type sklearn syntax from memory.

right.head: Scaffold, then audit
right.body: "AI-scaffolded" defined: a first-draft pipeline written by prompting an AI assistant (e.g., "fit a LinearRegression on these three features and print MAE/RMSE/R2"), which YOU then run, read, and interrogate — the same posture used since Week 4.

slides.teaching: This is explicitly where the plan wants AI-assisted scaffolding, not a hand-typed-from-scratch pipeline — say so, then move fast to the next two slides.

slides.title: LinearRegression, defined
slides.definition: Finds one coefficient per feature plus an intercept so predicted_eui = intercept + c1·wwr + c2·shade_m + c3·glazing_shgc fits the 105 training rows as closely as possible (least-squares).

example.head: .fit() and .predict()
example.body: model.fit(X_train, y_train) learns coef_ and intercept_ from training rows only. model.predict(X_test) then applies that SAME formula to the 35 held-out rows — no re-fitting, no peeking.

slides.teaching: Emphasize predict() reuses coefficients learned only from training rows — this is what makes the test-set metrics honest.

slides.title: The AI-scaffolded fit — three honest features
slides.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
pred = model.predict(X_test)

print("coef_:", np.round(model.coef_, 4))
print(f"intercept_: {model.intercept_:.4f}")
scores = report_metrics(y_test, pred, "3-feature")
slides.explainBody: The fitted directions are plausible for this dataset: higher wwr and SHGC associate with higher predicted EUI, while deeper shading associates with lower predicted EUI. These are conditional associations, not causal effects; magnitudes depend on units, scaling, omitted variables, and the sampled portfolio. R²≈0.49 shows useful but incomplete predictive signal.
slides.teaching: Ask students to say 'associated with,' not 'causes.' Read each coefficient with its unit and remind the class that an omitted variable can change signs and magnitudes.

slides.title: Beating the baseline — for real, not by magic
slides.callout: MAE drops ~21.5% (2.8906 → 2.2680). R² rises from ~0 to 0.4937. Real, but imperfect — the honest reason why is next.
slides.teaching: State the improvement is genuine and modest, not manufactured — set up over/underfitting and the leakage contrast still to come.

slides.title: MAE, defined
slides.definition: Mean Absolute Error: the average of |actual − predicted| across all 35 test rows, in the SAME units as the target (kWh/m2/yr). MAE=2.2680 means the model is off by about 2.27 kWh/m2/yr on average.

example.head: Reading it
example.body: Every residual counts equally, regardless of sign or size — a 1-unit miss and a 5-unit miss each contribute in proportion to their size, with no extra penalty for large errors.

slides.note: RMSE (next slide) squares each residual before averaging, so a few large misses pull it up more than MAE does — same units, different sensitivity to outliers.
slides.teaching: MAE is the metric students will hand-compute in Meeting B — keep the definition concrete and arithmetic.

slides.title: RMSE, defined
slides.definition: Root Mean Squared Error: square each residual, average the squares, take the square root. Same units as the target (kWh/m2/yr) — RMSE=2.7146.

example.head: Why it differs from MAE
example.body: Squaring means large residuals count MUCH more than small ones. RMSE (2.7146) > MAE (2.2680) here — a small signal that at least a few residuals (like V037's -6.34) are noticeably larger than the typical miss.

slides.note: MAE (previous slide) treats every residual proportionally; squaring is why RMSE (2.7146) sits above MAE (2.2680) here.
slides.teaching: Use RMSE > MAE here as the first hint that a residual plot is worth looking at — sets up the next few slides.

slides.title: R², defined
slides.definition: Coefficient of determination: the fraction of the target's variance the model explains, on a scale where 1.0 is a perfect fit and 0 is "no better than predicting the mean." R²=0.4937 here.

example.head: Reading it here
example.body: 0.4937 means this model accounts for about half of why EUI varies across the 140 variants. The other half is real, physical variation this 3-feature model cannot see yet (compactness, orientation).

slides.note: Reconnect to the baseline: R²≈-0.00003 there. Same metric, same scale, night-and-day difference.
slides.teaching: Reconnect explicitly to the baseline's R²≈-0.00003 — same metric, same scale, night-and-day difference.

slides.title: Residual, defined
slides.definition: residual = actual − predicted, computed for each test row. A positive residual means the model UNDER-predicted (actual was higher); negative means it OVER-predicted.

example.head: Why plot every one
example.body: A single MAE/RMSE number can hide a pattern — e.g., the model consistently over-predicting one kind of design. Plotting every residual against its predicted value is how you check for that pattern directly.

slides.note: The next two slides use this deck's real test-set residuals — first the full scatter, then the three largest misses (V037, V133, V043) diagnosed by hand.
slides.teaching: Tell students the next slide plots all 35 test-set residuals — not a summary statistic, the raw list.

slides.title: Residuals, plotted against predicted EUI
slides.chartTitle: Test-set residual (actual − predicted) vs. predicted EUI
slides.explainHead: No obvious pattern — a good sign
slides.explainBody: Residuals scatter both above and below zero across the whole predicted range, with no funnel or slope pattern. Three points sit clearly below the rest (V037, V133, V043, next slide) — real, diagnosable misses, not a systematic flaw.
slides.teaching: All 35 (predicted, residual) pairs are the actual verified test-set values from the pinned course environment, sorted by predicted value — not hand-copied or shortened.

slides.title: The three largest misses — diagnosable, not random
slides.callout: V037: the model over-predicts by 6.34 — it thinks this design performs worse than it actually does. V037 has deep shading (0.917, among the deepest) AND north orientation (coolest offset) — both real effects a 3-feature model without orientation cannot see.
slides.teaching: These are the exact verified worst-3 residuals from data/README.md; orientation isn't even a numeric feature yet in this model — only compactness gets added in Week 14.

slides.title: Underfitting, defined
slides.definition: The model is too simple to capture the real pattern — high error on BOTH the training set and the test set.

example.head: A mild, honest example
example.body: A model missing an obviously important feature — like this one, before compactness/orientation are added in Week 14 — is a mild, honest example of underfitting.

slides.note: Overfitting (next slide) is the opposite signature: low training error but much higher test error — same train/test comparison, opposite result.
slides.teaching: Keep this brief; overfitting next slide is the more surprising half of the pair.

slides.title: Overfitting, defined
slides.definition: The model fits the training rows' noise, not just their pattern — LOW error on training data but noticeably HIGHER error on the held-out test set. It has "memorized" rather than learned.

example.head: How you catch it
example.body: train_test_split is exactly how you catch this — compare training-set error against test-set error. A big gap between them is the signature of overfitting.

slides.note: Watch the next two slides for a THIRD case you haven't named yet — a model that looks TOO good on the test set, which is its own kind of red flag.
slides.teaching: Preview the predict slide next as a third case students haven't named yet: a model that looks TOO good on the test set — which is its own kind of red flag, not a success.

slides.title: What happens if you ask outside the training range?
slides.code:
# training data: wwr ranges 0.201–0.592
pred = model.predict([[0.85, 0.60, 0.45]])
print(pred)
slides.question: wwr=0.85 is far outside the training range. What prints?
options: An error — wwr is out of range
NaN — sklearn can't compute past its training data
36.13 — a normal-looking number, no warning at all
A warning message, then the number
slides.why: sklearn never checks the input's range. 36.13 looks ordinary, nothing visibly different — that silence itself is the danger.
slides.teaching: Freshly verified against the pinned course environment (a new illustrative input, not the unspecified wwr=0.85 example in data/README.md): model.predict([[0.85, 0.60, 0.45]]) using the exact verified coef_/intercept_ above returns 36.1307. Training X_train's wwr range is 0.201–0.592.

slides.title: Does one more feature really make R² this much better?
slides.code:
features_leak = ["wwr", "shade_m", "glazing_shgc",
                 "est_annual_cost_index"]
leak_model = LinearRegression().fit(Xtr_l, ytr_l)
pred_l = leak_model.predict(Xte_l)
print(f"R2: {r2_score(yte_l, pred_l):.4f}")
slides.question: Add est_annual_cost_index as a 4th feature. R²?
slides.why: R²=0.9923 is not a smarter model — est_annual_cost_index IS eui_kwh_m2yr in disguise. A jump this size is the leakage red flag itself.
slides.teaching: Verified against the pinned course environment and data/README.md: leak model R2=0.9923 vs honest model's 0.4937 — a jump of +0.4986. Take a show of hands on every option before revealing; option B (modest rise) is what a genuinely helpful new feature looks like — contrast explicitly with the next slide's actual output.

slides.title: The AI-drafted "improvement": one more feature
slides.code:
# AI-drafted, reasoning: "cost is a design-relevant
# variable too
features_leak = ["wwr", "shade_m", "glazing_shgc",
                 "est_annual_cost_index"]
X_leak = df[features_leak]
Xtr_l, Xte_l, ytr_l, yte_l = train_test_split(
    X_leak, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)

leak_model = LinearRegression().fit(Xtr_l, ytr_l)
pred_l = leak_model.predict(Xte_l)
print("coef_:", np.round(leak_model.coef_, 4))
slides.explainHead: The three honest coefficients just collapsed
slides.explainBody: wwr/shade_m/shgc's coefficients shrank to almost nothing (0.331, 0.0374, 0.3054, down from 17.6545, -3.3915, 3.4181); est_annual_cost_index's coefficient (7.1264) now does nearly all the work. Nothing about the CODE looks wrong — same split, same random_state=42, same LinearRegression call. The next slide scores it.
slides.teaching: Verified against the pinned course environment: coef_ [0.3310, 0.0374, 0.3054, 7.1264] — matches data/README.md exactly. Do not reveal the metrics yet; ask the room what the collapsed coefficients alone might already imply.

slides.title: ...continued: the metrics that AI-drafted code reported
slides.code:
mae_l = mean_absolute_error(yte_l, pred_l)
rmse_l = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(yte_l, pred_l))
r2_l = r2_score(yte_l, pred_l)

print(f"MAE:  {mae_l:.4f}")
print(f"RMSE: {rmse_l:.4f}")
print(f"R2:   {r2_l:.4f}")
slides.explainHead: R²=0.9923 is not good news — it's a red flag
slides.explainBody: wwr/shade_m/shgc's coefficients shrank to almost nothing; est_annual_cost_index's coefficient (7.1264) now does nearly all the work. An R² this close to 1.0 on a noisy, real-world-style target is the "too good to be true" signal ITSELF — be suspicious of a suspiciously perfect metric, not just hunting for a code pattern.
slides.teaching: Verified against the pinned course environment: MAE 0.2852, RMSE 0.3342, R2 0.9923 — matches data/README.md exactly. This is the SAME leakage bug students find and fix in Meeting B's studio — it is the graded task, not a bonus. Note the draft recomputes all three metrics inline instead of calling report_metrics; nothing is wrong with that, but it means nobody compared it against the baseline.

slides.title: Data leakage, defined
slides.definition: A feature that is (directly or nearly) DERIVED FROM the target, so the model isn't predicting — it's decoding the answer from a disguised copy of itself.

example.head: The proof, here
example.body: est_annual_cost_index = eui_kwh_m2yr × 0.14 + small noise — verified correlation with eui_kwh_m2yr = 0.995574. It is the target, wearing a different unit.

slides.teaching: Correlation 0.995574 verified against the pinned course environment by direct df[...].corr(df[...]) — matches data/README.md exactly.

slides.title: THE FIX, and why the AI drafted the bug

left.head: THE FIX
left.body: Drop est_annual_cost_index from the feature list entirely — it is a legitimate reporting/output column, never a predictor. Refit on the honest 3 features; MAE/RMSE/R² return to 2.2680 / 2.7146 / 0.4937.

right.head: Why the reasoning sounded plausible
right.body: "Cost is a design-relevant variable too" sounds reasonable — that is exactly why leakage is dangerous: it slips past a plausibility check. Checking a column's PROVENANCE (how was it computed?) catches what a plausibility read cannot.

slides.teaching: Silent extrapolation now has its own predict slide earlier in this deck — do not re-derive it here, just reinforce the provenance-check habit this slide is making.

slides.title: The whole week, as one documented function
slides.code:
def fit_and_score(features: list, label: str) -> dict:
    """Split, fit and score one list of features."""
    Xf = df[features]
    Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(
        Xf, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)
    fitted = LinearRegression().fit(Xtr, ytr)
    pred = fitted.predict(Xte)
    return report_metrics(yte, pred, label)
slides.explainHead: Split, fit, predict, score — for any feature list
slides.explainBody: Everything today's lecture did by hand, four separate times, is now eight lines: give it a feature list and a label, get back the same dictionary of three metrics. features: list and label: str are the type hints, -> dict is the return type, and the docstring states the job in one line. Because the split settings live INSIDE the function, no caller can slip in a different test_size or random_state — the next slide's comparison is guaranteed fair.
slides.teaching: Read the function aloud line by line before running it. Ask which earlier slide each line replaces (13, 15, 18, 30). Nothing prints — defining a function stores it; the next slide calls it three times.

slides.title: ...continued: three feature lists, one honest comparison
slides.code:
honest = fit_and_score(FEATURES3, "honest")
leaky = fit_and_score(features_leak, "leaky")
fixed = fit_and_score(FEATURES3, "fixed")

jump = leaky["R2"] - honest["R2"]
print("R2 jump:", round(jump, 4))
assert fixed["MAE"] == honest["MAE"]
slides.explainHead: The entire lecture, in four printed lines
slides.explainBody: Line 1 is the honest model. Line 2 is the AI's "improvement" — +0.4986 of R² bought entirely by a column derived from the target. Line 3 is the fix: drop the leaking feature, refit, and the honest numbers come back EXACTLY, which the final assert proves rather than asserts in prose. If that assert ever raised an AssertionError, the fix would not have been a fix.
slides.teaching: Verified against the pinned course environment: honest/fixed MAE=2.2680 RMSE=2.7146 R2=0.49374 (0.4937 to 4 decimals, matching data/README.md); leaky MAE=0.2852 RMSE=0.3342 R2=0.99233 (0.9923); R2 jump 0.4986. The assert passes silently — ask what its silence is actually claiming.

slides.title: Diagnose before you trust the metric
slides.prompt: A classmate's AI-scaffolded model reports R²=0.97 on this same eui_kwh_m2yr target, using 5 features that include est_annual_cost_index. Is this a good model?
steps: State your prediction: legitimate improvement, or a red flag — and why?
Check: is any feature DERIVED from the target itself, not just correlated with it?
Recall the correlation between est_annual_cost_index and eui_kwh_m2yr from this deck.
State the fix in one sentence, and what MAE/RMSE/R² you would expect after it.
slides.teaching: Verified answer: red flag, not an improvement; correlation 0.995574; fix = drop est_annual_cost_index; expected metrics return to MAE=2.2680, RMSE=2.7146, R2=0.4937 — the exact honest 3-feature numbers from earlier in this deck.

slides.title: Fit fast. Trust only after you audit.
takeaways: A naive baseline (predict the mean) comes first — MAE=2.8906, R²≈-0.00003 defines "no better than guessing."
The AI-scaffolded 3-feature LinearRegression genuinely beats it: MAE=2.2680, R²=0.4937 — real, honest, imperfect.
MAE, RMSE, R², and a residual plot are how you read HOW wrong a model still is — not just whether it "works."
A suspiciously high R² (0.9923 here) is not good news — it is the signal to check every feature's provenance for leakage.
slides.teaching: Exit ticket: students name, in one sentence, how they would check a NEW feature for leakage before adding it to next week's model.
